Research begins with a real question

Choose an argument worth testing.

Each prompt pairs a contested historical question with defensible positions and a source map. Choose one prompt and one numbered position, refine it into your own thesis, and use the mapped evidence as a launch point—not a checklist.

Writer’s guide

From question to historical argument

01

Choose

Select one prompt and one numbered position. You may refine the position, but your thesis must answer the prompt directly.

02

Research

Use the source map as a launch point. Build an argument from primary evidence and historical scholarship. Start with sources listed for your position, then read at least one source for a rival position so you can answer it as the Counter-Argument.

03

Cite

Cite the historical document, book, journal article, or original web publication—never this page or an archive page as the source locator.

04

Interpret

Read each source for its argument and its limits. [IMAGE] marks a visual source. [RETROSPECTIVE] marks later testimony. [OUTSIDE DATES] marks evidence outside the prompt’s focus range; use it only for context or comparison and name the limitation.

Read the note on dropped and reworded options

Why some familiar arguments are missing. Every numbered position in this set is backed by enough primary sources, books, and journal articles in your readers to defend it. The positions below were dropped or reworded so that you never cite a historian for a claim the historian does not make.

  • 18.6.3 · Why Farmers Revolted — This position was reworded so that it matches what the historians in your readers actually argue. Defend it as written here, not in its older, stronger form.
  • 18.8.1 · Civil Service Reform — This position was reworded so that it matches what the historians in your readers actually argue. Defend it as written here, not in its older, stronger form.
  • 19.10.2 · The Plan de San Diego — This position was reworded so that it matches what the historians in your readers actually argue. Defend it as written here, not in its older, stronger form.
  • 16.1 · Robber Barons or Captains of Industry? — Not offered as an option: Constructive “industrial statesmen” whose innovations brought order, efficiency, and lower prices to chaotic industries. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 17.1 · How New Was the New South? — Not offered as an option: The Lost Cause eased white Southerners’ acceptance of the New South rather than resisting it. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 17.6 · What Made the West? — Not offered as an option: Powerful Native nations such as the Lakotas and Comanches were themselves expansionist powers that shaped the West. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 17.7 · Federal Indian Policy — Not offered as an option: Well-meaning but paternalistic reform that failed. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 18.1 · Who Were the Populists? — Not offered as an option: Modernizing reformers who embraced science, organization, and a strong state. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 18.3 · The New Immigrants — Not offered as an option: Uprooted: migration was a wrenching break that left newcomers alienated. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 18.5 · The Reach of Social Darwinism — Not offered as an option: Evolutionary ideas popularized by Spencer and Sumner gave defenders of laissez-faire and wealth a scientific-sounding justification. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 18.7 · The Election of 1896 — Not offered as an option: Religion and ethnicity: Bryan’s evangelical crusade drove urban, immigrant, and liturgical voters to McKinley. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 18.7 · The Election of 1896 — Not offered as an option: The realignment idea itself is flawed. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 19.2 · Why War with Spain? — Not offered as an option: Gendered ideals of chivalry and manhood pushed Americans toward war. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 19.3 · Taking the Philippines — Not offered as an option: Commercial strategy: a stepping stone to the China market. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 19.3 · Taking the Philippines — Not offered as an option: A test of national manhood. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 19.4 · The Philippine–American War — Not offered as an option: A Filipino revolution and nation-making struggle, seen from below. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 19.5 · The Anti-Imperialists — Not offered as an option: “Anti-colonial imperialists”: they rejected colonies but backed an informal empire of trade. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 19.6 · The Annexation of Hawai‘i — Not offered as an option: Native Hawaiians resisted annexation and never consented to it. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • 19.10 · The Plan de San Diego — Not offered as an option: An uprising shaped by revolutionary Mexico’s radical ideology, especially the Magonistas’ anarchism. The readers do not yet hold enough scholarship that argues it. You may raise it as a Counter-Argument, but do not cite a historian for it unless that historian makes the claim.
  • Not offered as a prompt — Was the Haymarket trial a miscarriage of justice? The readers do not yet hold enough evidence on more than one side of this debate.
  • Not offered as a prompt — What destroyed the bison herds? The readers do not yet hold enough evidence on more than one side of this debate.
  • Not offered as a prompt — Were the greenback and free-silver reformers serious economic critics or monetary cranks? The readers do not yet hold enough evidence on more than one side of this debate.
  • Not offered as a prompt — Was the Populists’ 1896 fusion with the Democrats on free silver a betrayal of Populism or a sound strategy? The readers do not yet hold enough evidence on more than one side of this debate.
  • Not offered as a prompt — Were Chinese immigrants passive sojourners or active resisters of discrimination? The readers do not yet hold enough evidence on more than one side of this debate.

Chapter 16 · 1859–1901

16.1 · Robber Barons or Captains of Industry?

How should historians judge the industrialists who built Big Business in the late nineteenth century?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

How should historians judge the industrialists who built Big Business in the late nineteenth century?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 16.1.1 Robber barons: the great industrialists built their fortunes through fraud, monopoly, and the corruption of government.
  2. 16.1.2 Neither villains nor heroes: their genius and their ruthlessness have to be weighed together.
  3. 16.1.3 The system, not the men: Big Business grew out of new technology, national markets, and managerial organization more than out of any tycoon’s character.
  4. 16.1.4 Creatures of government: the great corporations depended on subsidy and political favor, and were often failures as businesses.
Keep in focus: 1865–1901. Judge the industrialists’ methods and their results, not just their wealth, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Were the men who built Big Business villains, heroes, or something else?

  • 16.1.1 They were crooks who got rich by cheating and buying politicians.
  • 16.1.2 They were both brilliant and ruthless, and both sides matter.
  • 16.1.3 Big companies came from new technology and organization, not from one man’s personality.
  • 16.1.4 Big companies lived off government help and were often badly run.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 16 · 1859–1901

16.2 · A Laissez-Faire Era?

Was the Gilded Age an era of laissez-faire, in which government stood aside and let business run the economy?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Was the Gilded Age an era of laissez-faire, in which government stood aside and let business run the economy?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 16.2.1 Largely laissez-faire: government left business unregulated, and the courts shielded property from reform.
  2. 16.2.2 An active developmental state: government subsidized, protected, and shaped the industrial economy.
  3. 16.2.3 An older legal tradition: the courts struck down laws as “class legislation,” following a long tradition rather than a new pro-business ideology.
Keep in focus: 1865–1900. Look at what federal, state, and court actions actually did to the economy, not only at what politicians and judges said about it.
In Plain Terms

Question: Did government really leave business alone in the Gilded Age?

  • 16.2.1 Yes: government mostly stayed out, and courts protected business from reformers.
  • 16.2.2 No: government actively helped build the economy with land, tariffs, and laws.
  • 16.2.3 Judges were following an old rule against laws that favored one group, not just siding with business.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 16 · 1859–1901

16.3 · Did Workers Gain?

Did industrialization improve the lives of American workers between 1865 and 1900?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Did industrialization improve the lives of American workers between 1865 and 1900?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 16.3.1 Yes, measurably: real wages and living standards rose substantially.
  2. 16.3.2 Gains with heavy costs: wage gains were offset by unemployment, industrial injury, and the loss of control over work.
  3. 16.3.3 A hidden biological cost: average height and health declined even as incomes grew.
Keep in focus: 1865–1900. Decide which measure of “better off” you are using (wages, security, health) and defend that choice.
In Plain Terms

Question: Were workers better off because of industrialization?

  • 16.3.1 Yes: workers earned more and could buy more.
  • 16.3.2 Wages rose, but jobs were unsafe and unsteady, and workers lost control of their work.
  • 16.3.3 People earned more but grew shorter and less healthy.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 16 · 1859–1901

16.4 · Why Craft Unionism?

Why did American labor turn toward the craft unionism of the American Federation of Labor instead of a broad labor or socialist movement?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Why did American labor turn toward the craft unionism of the American Federation of Labor instead of a broad labor or socialist movement?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 16.4.1 Workers’ own choice: American workers preferred “job-conscious” trade unionism suited to American abundance and opportunity.
  2. 16.4.2 The courts and the state: injunctions, court rulings, and repression pushed labor away from politics and broad solidarity.
  3. 16.4.3 Employers’ victory: organized employers defeated the Knights of Labor’s inclusive alternative.
  4. 16.4.4 Divided workers: racial and ethnic divisions fractured working-class solidarity.
  5. 16.4.5 A misframed question: American workers built radical, militant cultures as vigorous as Europe’s.
Keep in focus: 1869–1900. Explain the outcome, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging rather than listing every obstacle labor faced.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did American unions end up narrow and skilled-only instead of broad and political?

  • 16.4.1 Workers wanted better pay and hours, not a new society.
  • 16.4.2 Courts and government made broad, political unions too costly.
  • 16.4.3 Bosses organized and crushed the Knights of Labor.
  • 16.4.4 Workers were split by race and ethnicity.
  • 16.4.5 American workers were just as radical as Europeans; the question assumes too much.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 16 · 1859–1901

16.5 · The Great Strikes

What best explains the violence and defeat of the great strikes of 1877–1894?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

What best explains the violence and defeat of the great strikes of 1877–1894?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 16.5.1 State power: corporations backed by troops, injunctions, and private guards crushed the strikes.
  2. 16.5.2 Local politics: outcomes turned on local politics and how much support strikers had in their communities.
  3. 16.5.3 Fear of disorder: middle-class fear, inflamed by the press, turned public opinion against labor.
Keep in focus: 1877–1894. Use at least two of the great strikes (1877, Homestead, Pullman, and others) and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why were the big strikes so violent, and why did workers lose?

  • 16.5.1 Companies won because troops, courts, and hired guards were on their side.
  • 16.5.2 It depended on whether the town and local officials backed the strikers.
  • 16.5.3 Newspapers scared the middle class, who then turned against strikers.

16.6 · Women and Wage Work

Did industrial wage work liberate women or exploit them?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Did industrial wage work liberate women or exploit them?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 16.6.1 Liberation: wage work gave young women new independence and a public culture of their own.
  2. 16.6.2 Exploitation: sex-segregated, low-wage work reinforced women’s subordination.
  3. 16.6.3 It depended on race and class: for Black and immigrant women, wage work meant family survival and a site of resistance.
Keep in focus: 1865–1900. Say which women you are writing about, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Was factory and wage work good or bad for women?

  • 16.6.1 It gave young women their own money, freedom, and social life.
  • 16.6.2 It kept women in low-paid “women’s jobs” and under men’s control.
  • 16.6.3 For Black and immigrant women, work was about family survival and fighting back.

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.1 · How New Was the New South?

How new was the “New South” that boosters proclaimed after Reconstruction?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

How new was the “New South” that boosters proclaimed after Reconstruction?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.1.1 A new ruling class: commercial “Redeemers” displaced the planters but left the South a colonial economy of the North.
  2. 17.1.2 Planter persistence: the old planter elite survived and shaped Southern industry in its own interest.
  3. 17.1.3 A boosters’ myth: the New South was more a creed than a reality.
  4. 17.1.4 A low-wage labor market: an isolated regional labor market explains why the South lagged.
  5. 17.1.5 Real but uneven change: change came, but it varied sharply by place, race, and class.
Keep in focus: 1877–1900. Compare the New South with the Old South on at least one concrete measure (who held power, who owned industry, how labor worked).
In Plain Terms

Question: Did the South really change after Reconstruction?

  • 17.1.1 New businessmen took over, but the South stayed poor and dependent on the North.
  • 17.1.2 The old planters stayed in charge and ran the new industries their way.
  • 17.1.3 The “New South” was mostly talk and advertising.
  • 17.1.4 The South fell behind because its cheap labor was cut off from the rest of the country.
  • 17.1.5 Things changed, but very differently for different places and people.

17

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.2 · Trapped by the Crop Lien

Why did sharecropping and the crop-lien system trap so many Southern farmers in poverty?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Why did sharecropping and the crop-lien system trap so many Southern farmers in poverty?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.2.1 Merchant monopoly: local merchants’ monopolies and the crop lien created debt peonage.
  2. 17.2.2 Market forces: falling world cotton prices, more than exploitation, explain rural poverty.
  3. 17.2.3 Freedom turned to coercion: sharecropping began as freedpeople’s bid for autonomy, but law and violence turned it into a coercive labor system.
Keep in focus: 1865–1900. Explain the trap itself, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging rather than listing every hardship.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why couldn’t Southern farmers escape poverty?

  • 17.2.1 Store owners controlled credit and kept farmers in debt.
  • 17.2.2 Cotton prices fell worldwide; that, not cheating, made farmers poor.
  • 17.2.3 Freedpeople chose sharecropping for independence, but laws and violence turned it into a trap.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.3 · The Origins of Jim Crow

When and why did Jim Crow segregation take hold in the South?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

When and why did Jim Crow segregation take hold in the South?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.3.1 Late and not inevitable: segregation hardened in the 1890s, after other paths had been tried.
  2. 17.3.2 Early, by custom: segregation replaced outright exclusion and spread right after the war.
  3. 17.3.3 A modern system: segregation was bound up with cities, railroads, and consumer culture.
  4. 17.3.4 Built by law: legislatures and courts built segregation, culminating in “separate but equal.”
Keep in focus: 1877–1900. Your answer must address both when and why, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: When did segregation start in the South, and why?

  • 17.3.1 It came late, in the 1890s, and things could have gone differently.
  • 17.3.2 It started right after the war, as a step up from being shut out completely.
  • 17.3.3 It grew with new cities, trains, and stores.
  • 17.3.4 Laws and court decisions like Plessy built it.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.4 · Why Disfranchisement?

Why did Southern states strip Black men of the vote between 1890 and 1908?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Why did Southern states strip Black men of the vote between 1890 and 1908?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.4.1 Elite power: Democratic elites engineered disfranchisement to destroy political opposition, Black and white.
  2. 17.4.2 Answering fusion: a white-supremacy campaign, enforced by violence, answered the threat of Populist–Republican fusion.
  3. 17.4.3 Radical racism: disfranchisement expressed a deepening racism among white Southerners at large.
  4. 17.4.4 The story is resistance: Black Southerners kept political life alive through institutions and resistance despite disfranchisement.
Keep in focus: 1890–1908. Explain the motive behind the new laws, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did Southern states take away Black men’s right to vote?

  • 17.4.1 Powerful Democrats wanted to wipe out any opposition, including poor whites.
  • 17.4.2 It was a violent response to Black and white voters joining forces.
  • 17.4.3 Most white Southerners were becoming more extreme in their racism.
  • 17.4.4 The bigger story is how Black Southerners kept organizing anyway.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.5 · Judging Booker T. Washington

How should historians judge Booker T. Washington’s strategy of accommodation?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

How should historians judge Booker T. Washington’s strategy of accommodation?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.5.1 Too costly: accommodation conceded too much and helped entrench white supremacy.
  2. 17.5.2 Realism under terror: a realistic strategy combined with hidden resistance and institution building.
  3. 17.5.3 Uplift’s blind spots: the “uplift” ideology of Washington and his critics carried class and gender assumptions of its own.
Keep in focus: 1895–1915. Judge the strategy against the conditions Washington faced, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Was Booker T. Washington’s approach a mistake, a smart move, or something else?

  • 17.5.1 He gave up too much and helped white supremacy.
  • 17.5.2 It was smart under the threat of violence, and he secretly fought back.
  • 17.5.3 Both Washington and his critics had class and gender biases.

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.6 · What Made the West?

Was the American West made by the frontier experience, or by conquest, capital, and the federal government?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Was the American West made by the frontier experience, or by conquest, capital, and the federal government?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.6.1 The frontier: the frontier experience forged American individualism and democracy.
  2. 17.6.2 Conquest: the West was a place of conquest directed by the federal government, whose legacy continues.
  3. 17.6.3 A meeting ground: the West was a meeting ground of many peoples, not a single Euro-American frontier.
  4. 17.6.4 Capital and markets: Eastern capital, cities, and markets remade the western landscape.
  5. 17.6.5 A national myth: the frontier was above all a story the nation told about itself, from Turner to Buffalo Bill.
Keep in focus: 1865–1900. Name which interpretive tradition you are engaging, and use at least one western place or people as your test case.
In Plain Terms

Question: What really shaped the American West?

  • 17.6.1 Settling the frontier made Americans independent and democratic.
  • 17.6.2 The West was conquered, with the federal government in charge.
  • 17.6.3 Many different peoples met and mixed there.
  • 17.6.4 Eastern money and city markets reshaped the West.
  • 17.6.5 The “frontier” was mostly a myth Americans told about themselves.

Source Map

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.7 · Federal Indian Policy

How should federal Indian policy after the Civil War be understood?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

How should federal Indian policy after the Civil War be understood?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.7.1 Dispossession: assimilation policy as dispossession and cultural destruction.
  2. 17.7.2 Settler colonialism: policy as settler colonialism and genocide.
  3. 17.7.3 Native survival: Native peoples adapted, resisted, and survived on their own terms.
Keep in focus: 1865–1900. Use at least one specific policy (reservations, allotment, boarding schools) and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: What was U.S. policy toward Native Americans really about?

  • 17.7.1 It took Native land and tried to erase Native cultures.
  • 17.7.2 It was a campaign to replace Native peoples, even by killing them.
  • 17.7.3 Native peoples found ways to resist and survive.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 17 · 1859–1900

17.8 · How Wild Was the West?

Was the American West unusually violent?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Was the American West unusually violent?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 17.8.1 Yes, distinctively: the West bred a culture of violence and vigilantism.
  2. 17.8.2 Largely a myth: the gunfighter West is mostly legend; cattle towns saw few killings.
  3. 17.8.3 Racial violence: the worst violence was the lynching and expulsion of Mexican Americans, Chinese, and Native peoples.
Keep in focus: 1865–1900. Say what kind of violence you are measuring and whom it struck, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Was the Wild West really that violent?

  • 17.8.1 Yes: the West had its own culture of shootings and mob justice.
  • 17.8.2 No: the gunfighter stories are mostly made up.
  • 17.8.3 The worst violence was against people of color.

Did the American West liberate women?

  2. 17.9.2 Old burdens: women carried traditional domestic roles west and bore heavy burdens there.

  • 17.9.1 Yes: the West gave women new jobs and roles.

Chapter 18 · 1859–1898

18.2 · Empty Politics or Real Conflict?

Was Gilded Age politics an empty contest of spoilsmen or a meaningful clash over real issues?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Was Gilded Age politics an empty contest of spoilsmen or a meaningful clash over real issues?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 18.2.1 Empty politics: an issueless era of corrupt, interchangeable parties.
  2. 18.2.2 Religion and ethnicity: party loyalty was rooted in voters’ religion and ethnicity.
  3. 18.2.3 Real battles: the parties fought over tariffs, money, and federal power.
  4. 18.2.4 Mass participation: a politics of spectacle and loyalty drew record turnouts.
Keep in focus: 1877–1896. Use at least one election or policy fight as evidence, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Did Gilded Age politics matter?

  • 18.2.1 No: the parties were corrupt and basically the same.
  • 18.2.2 People voted by their church and ethnic group.
  • 18.2.3 Yes: the parties really fought over big economic questions.
  • 18.2.4 Politics was a popular show that brought huge crowds to vote.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 18 · 1859–1898

18.3 · The New Immigrants

Were the “new immigrants” of 1880–1910 uprooted, transplanted, or transnational?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Were the “new immigrants” of 1880–1910 uprooted, transplanted, or transnational?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 18.3.1 A melting pot: newcomers assimilated into a new American people.
  2. 18.3.2 Transplanted: families and communities used old-world networks and values to adapt.
  3. 18.3.3 Transnational: many migrants moved back and forth and kept ties across borders.
Keep in focus: 1880–1910. Use at least one immigrant group as your test case, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: How did immigrants experience moving to America?

  • 18.3.1 They blended in and became Americans.
  • 18.3.2 They used families and old-country ways to adjust.
  • 18.3.3 Many went back and forth and kept ties to home.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 18 · 1859–1898

18.4 · Chinese Exclusion

What drove the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

What drove the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 18.4.1 Labor’s demand: white workers and labor organizations demanded exclusion.
  2. 18.4.2 Politicians: national politicians chasing votes, more than workers, drove exclusion.
  3. 18.4.3 Race and the gatekeeping nation: racial ideology and the building of a “gatekeeping” nation produced exclusion.
  4. 18.4.4 Violence and diplomacy: anti-Chinese violence in the West, and its diplomatic fallout, produced exclusion.
Keep in focus: 1870–1882. Explain why exclusion became national law, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did the United States ban Chinese immigration?

  • 18.4.1 White workers pushed for it.
  • 18.4.2 Politicians pushed it to win votes.
  • 18.4.3 Racism, and a new idea of guarding the border, drove it.
  • 18.4.4 Attacks on Chinese people in the West, and trouble with China, led to it.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 18 · 1859–1898

18.5 · The Reach of Social Darwinism

How influential was Social Darwinism in Gilded Age America?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

How influential was Social Darwinism in Gilded Age America?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 18.5.1 Largely a myth: few businessmen or thinkers actually argued from it.
  2. 18.5.2 Put to other uses: evolutionary ideas were used even more by reformers and racial scientists.
Keep in focus: 1870–1900. Distinguish what writers like Spencer and Sumner argued from how others used evolutionary language, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Did “survival of the fittest” ideas really shape the Gilded Age?

  • 18.5.1 No: hardly anyone really believed or used it.
  • 18.5.2 Reformers and race scientists used these ideas more than businessmen did.

Chapter 18 · 1859–1898

18.6 · Why Farmers Revolted

Why did American farmers revolt in the late nineteenth century?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Why did American farmers revolt in the late nineteenth century?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 18.6.1 Real exploitation: railroads, merchants, and bankers exploited farmers.
  2. 18.6.2 Commercialization and risk: farmers’ terms of trade were not worsening; protest reflected the risks of commercial farming.
  3. 18.6.3 Deflation: the gold standard’s falling prices, which favored creditors and Northeastern finance, raised the real burden of farmers’ debts.
Keep in focus: 1870–1896. Use economic evidence (prices, debt, freight rates, credit) and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why were farmers so angry?

  • 18.6.1 Railroads, merchants, and banks really were cheating them.
  • 18.6.2 Prices weren’t actually worse; farmers were upset by the risks of farming for markets.
  • 18.6.3 Falling prices under gold made farm debts harder to pay.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 19 · 1867–1917

19.2 · Why War with Spain?

Why did the United States go to war with Spain in 1898?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Why did the United States go to war with Spain in 1898?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 19.2.1 The press and the public: the yellow press and public hysteria pushed the nation into war.
  2. 19.2.2 McKinley’s design: McKinley led deliberately toward war to secure national interests.
  3. 19.2.3 Political pressure: domestic pressure on McKinley and Congress made war unavoidable.
  4. 19.2.4 Controlling Cuba: the United States intervened to control Cuba’s own independence struggle.
Keep in focus: 1895–1898. Explain the decision for war, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did the United States fight Spain in 1898?

  • 19.2.1 Sensational newspapers whipped up the public.
  • 19.2.2 McKinley planned the path to war on purpose.
  • 19.2.3 Political pressure at home left no choice.
  • 19.2.4 The U.S. stepped in to control Cuba’s fight for independence.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 19 · 1867–1917

19.3 · Taking the Philippines

Why did the United States annex the Philippines?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

Why did the United States annex the Philippines?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 19.3.1 Racial paternalism: “benevolent assimilation” and the “white man’s burden.”
  2. 19.3.2 McKinley’s deliberate choice: a step-by-step decision weighing strategic and political realities rather than any single motive.
Keep in focus: 1898–1902. Explain the decision to annex, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did the United States take the Philippines?

  • 19.3.1 Americans thought they had a duty to rule and “uplift” Filipinos.
  • 19.3.2 McKinley decided step by step, weighing many factors.

Chapter 19 · 1867–1917

19.6 · The Annexation of Hawai‘i

How should the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy and the annexation of Hawai‘i be understood?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

How should the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy and the annexation of Hawai‘i be understood?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 19.6.1 The planters: American sugar planters and businessmen engineered the overthrow and annexation for their own gain.
  2. 19.6.2 Washington’s calculations: strategic and racial calculations in Washington decided whether and when to annex.
Keep in focus: 1887–1898. Explain who decided Hawai‘i’s fate, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Who was responsible for the United States taking Hawai‘i?

  • 19.6.1 American sugar planters took it for profit.
  • 19.6.2 Leaders in Washington decided, for military and racial reasons.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 19 · 1867–1917

19.7 · The Big Stick

What drove Theodore Roosevelt’s “big stick” and U.S. interventions in Latin America?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

What drove Theodore Roosevelt’s “big stick” and U.S. interventions in Latin America?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 19.7.1 Realism: a pursuit of security, order, and great-power standing.
  2. 19.7.2 Dollar diplomacy: economic imperialism and the protection of U.S. investment.
  3. 19.7.3 Race and manliness: ideas of race, civilization, and manliness drove intervention.
  4. 19.7.4 Latin American agency: Latin Americans and canal workers shaped outcomes through their own politics and resistance.
Keep in focus: 1901–1913. Use at least one intervention (Panama, the Dominican Republic, Cuba, Nicaragua) and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did the United States keep intervening in Latin America?

  • 19.7.1 For security and to act like a great power.
  • 19.7.2 To protect American money and business.
  • 19.7.3 Ideas about race and manhood drove it.
  • 19.7.4 Latin Americans shaped what happened through their own actions.

Source Map

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.

Chapter 19 · 1867–1917

19.10 · The Plan de San Diego

What explains the Plan de San Diego uprising of 1915 and its violent suppression?

HIST C1002 · Unit 5 · Growing Pains

What explains the Plan de San Diego uprising of 1915 and its violent suppression?

Choose and defend one of the following positions (or stake out a qualified position between two):

  1. 19.10.1 Dispossession and terror: a rebellion rooted in Tejano dispossession and answered by Anglo and Ranger terror.
  2. 19.10.2 Diplomatic leverage: a plot entangled in U.S.–Mexican diplomacy that Carranza used as leverage for U.S. recognition.
Keep in focus: 1915–1916. Explain both the uprising and the response to it, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did the Plan de San Diego uprising happen, and why was it crushed so violently?

  • 19.10.1 Tejanos who had lost their land rebelled, and Rangers answered with terror.
  • 19.10.2 Mexico’s Carranza used it to pressure the U.S.

Select an identifier to open its source page in The Garza Archive. Each source is labeled for the positions it serves: supports, qualifies, challenges, or counters. A source that counters your position is a Counter-Argument to answer.
